title: Cisplatin: Kidneys, Hearing, Nerves, and Hydration
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Cisplatin is a platinum antineoplastic with major cumulative renal, neurologic, auditory, gastrointestinal, and marrow toxicity. Safe nursing care centers hydration, renal/electrolyte surveillance, hearing/neuropathy cues, antiemetic support, and prompt escalation of infection or kidney injury.
recognize: Rising creatinine, falling urine output, magnesium wasting, tinnitus/hearing change, distal numbness, severe nausea/vomiting, or cytopenias can reflect toxicity.
Renal toxicity becomes more likely with cumulative exposure, poor hydration, baseline renal impairment, and other nephrotoxic drugs.
priorities: Verify ordered hydration and current renal/electrolyte data before therapy.
Assess hearing/neurologic symptoms and infection/bleeding risk.
Escalate acute kidney injury, severe electrolyte abnormality, new hearing loss, or febrile neutropenia.
assessMonitor: Trend creatinine/clearance, BUN, magnesium and other electrolytes, urine output, CBC, nausea/vomiting, neuropathy, and hearing symptoms.
interventions: Implement ordered hydration and antiemetic plans and protect reliable venous access.
medicationSafety: Avoid assuming hydration completely prevents nephrotoxicity.
Review concurrent nephrotoxic and ototoxic medications during reconciliation.
teaching: Report decreased urine, tinnitus/hearing change, numbness/tingling, fever, or uncontrolled vomiting promptly.
delegationScope: Chemotherapy administration authority varies by state/facility and usually requires specialty competency; PN care should emphasize ordered monitoring, supportive care, and rapid escalation.
examTrap: Focusing on nausea while missing rising creatinine and magnesium loss.
oneLinePearl: With cisplatin, protect the kidneys and listen for the ears and nerves.

title: Doxorubicin: Cardiac Function and Vesicant Safety
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Doxorubicin is an anthracycline with cumulative cardiomyopathy risk, severe myelosuppression, and vesicant extravasation injury. New dyspnea, edema, reduced exercise tolerance, or burning/swelling at the IV site deserves immediate attention.
recognize: Cardiotoxicity can be subclinical before symptomatic heart failure develops.
Extravasation can produce severe tissue necrosis, and marrow suppression increases infection/bleeding risk.
priorities: Confirm cardiac-monitoring plan and reliable IV/central access according to protocol.
Stop administration and activate the extravasation protocol for suspected leakage.
Escalate heart-failure symptoms, severe cytopenia complications, or significant mucositis.
assessMonitor: Trend LVEF when ordered, BP, dyspnea/edema, CBC, mucosal integrity, infection signs, and infusion-site status.
interventions: Use vesicant precautions and specialty chemotherapy-handling procedures.
medicationSafety: Cumulative dose and concomitant cardiotoxic therapies affect cardiac risk.
Red/orange urine can occur after treatment and is not by itself hematuria, but persistent or symptomatic urinary change still needs evaluation.
teaching: Report shortness of breath, swelling, fever, mouth sores, or IV-site pain immediately.
delegationScope: Vesicant chemotherapy administration requires facility/state competency; suspected extravasation or cardiotoxicity requires immediate RN/provider/oncology escalation.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient about IV-site burning because the line still flushes.
oneLinePearl: Doxorubicin threatens the heart and the tissue around a leaking IV.
sourceBasis: DailyMed doxorubicin hydrochloride prescribing information updated 2026-05

title: Cyclophosphamide: Marrow Suppression and Hemorrhagic Cystitis
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Cyclophosphamide can cause severe myelosuppression and urotoxicity including hemorrhagic cystitis. Hydration, frequent bladder emptying when prescribed, urine/hematuria surveillance, CBC monitoring, and mesna when ordered are central safety measures.
recognize: Dysuria, hematuria, pelvic pain, or urinary frequency can signal bladder injury.
Neutropenia and thrombocytopenia increase infection and bleeding risk.
priorities: Review CBC and urinary/renal status before treatment.
Implement ordered hydration/mesna and encourage regular voiding when appropriate.
Escalate gross hematuria, severe bladder pain, fever, or significant marrow suppression.
assessMonitor: Trend CBC, urinalysis/hematuria, urine output, renal function, hydration status, infection, and bleeding.
interventions: Support oral/IV hydration as ordered and avoid urinary retention during treatment.
medicationSafety: Mesna reduces urotoxicity but does not eliminate all cyclophosphamide toxicities.
Active urinary obstruction should be identified before therapy.
teaching: Report blood in urine, painful urination, fever, or unusual bleeding promptly and follow the prescribed hydration/voiding plan.
delegationScope: Chemotherapy administration requires specialty competency; urinary and marrow-toxicity findings require licensed-nurse assessment and escalation.
examTrap: Assuming mesna means bladder monitoring is no longer necessary.
oneLinePearl: Cyclophosphamide safety means watch the marrow and the bladder.

title: Vincristine: IV Only—Fatal if Given Intrathecally
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Vincristine is a vinca alkaloid for intravenous use only. Intrathecal administration is usually fatal, making route segregation and verification one of the highest-priority medication-safety checks in oncology.
recognize: Peripheral/autonomic neuropathy can cause weakness, paresthesia, constipation or ileus.
Extravasation can cause significant local tissue injury.
priorities: Verify the IV-only route and product labeling before administration.
Assess neurologic and bowel function and the IV site.
Escalate any route discrepancy, extravasation, ileus, severe neuropathy, or suspected intrathecal error as an emergency.
assessMonitor: Trend strength/sensation, reflexes, bowel pattern, abdominal distention, CBC, and infusion-site status.
interventions: Maintain strict separation from intrathecal medications and follow institutional vincristine safety systems.
medicationSafety: Current labeling states IV use only and fatal if given by other routes.
Dose-limiting toxicity is often neurologic rather than severe marrow suppression.
teaching: Report new numbness, weakness, severe constipation, or abdominal swelling.
delegationScope: Vincristine administration requires oncology competency; route verification cannot be delegated away from accountable licensed clinicians.
examTrap: Treating vincristine like any other chemotherapy bag when an intrathecal procedure is occurring nearby.
oneLinePearl: Vincristine has one route: IV—anything else can be fatal.
sourceBasis: DailyMed vincristine sulfate injection labeling current 2026

title: Fluorouracil: DPD Deficiency, Cardiotoxicity, and Mucositis
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Fluorouracil can cause life-threatening toxicity in complete DPD deficiency and can also produce cardiotoxicity, severe diarrhea/mucositis, myelosuppression, neurotoxicity, and hand-foot syndrome. Early unusually severe toxicity is a major warning signal.
recognize: New chest pain during infusion can represent fluorouracil cardiotoxicity.
Early severe diarrhea, mucositis, confusion/ataxia, or profound cytopenias may suggest excessive exposure including DPD deficiency.
priorities: Review ordered DPYD/DPD evaluation and baseline CBC/organ status.
Escalate chest pain, acute neuro change, severe diarrhea/mucositis, or unusually early severe toxicity immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend CBC, hydration, diarrhea, oral mucosa, skin of palms/soles, neurologic status, and cardiac symptoms.
interventions: Provide meticulous oral/skin care and hydration support according to the treatment plan.
medicationSafety: Current U.S. labeling carries a boxed warning for serious adverse reactions or death with complete DPD deficiency.
Warfarin interaction can increase INR and bleeding risk.
teaching: Report chest pain, severe diarrhea, mouth sores, confusion, or fever immediately rather than waiting for the next oncology visit.
delegationScope: Chemotherapy administration requires specialty competency; toxicity recognition/supportive care and escalation must follow oncology protocols.
examTrap: Assuming severe diarrhea and mucositis are expected enough to wait until the next scheduled assessment.
oneLinePearl: Early severe 5-FU toxicity is not routine—think DPD and escalate.

title: Paclitaxel: Hypersensitivity and Neuropathy Monitoring
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Paclitaxel can cause severe hypersensitivity reactions despite premedication, along with myelosuppression and cumulative peripheral neuropathy. The nurse must be ready to stop the infusion and treat anaphylaxis while also tracking marrow and neurologic toxicity between cycles.
recognize: Dyspnea, hypotension, angioedema, urticaria, or wheezing during infusion can signal severe hypersensitivity.
Progressive numbness/tingling can become function-limiting neuropathy.
priorities: Confirm premedication and emergency readiness before infusion.
Monitor closely during administration, especially early exposure.
Stop/escalate severe hypersensitivity, febrile neutropenia, or progressive motor/sensory dysfunction.
assessMonitor: Trend CBC, infusion reaction signs, neuropathy, infection, hepatic context, and functional impact.
interventions: Follow specialty infusion and hypersensitivity protocols.
medicationSafety: Premedication lowers but does not eliminate anaphylaxis risk.
Neuropathy should be assessed before repeated dosing rather than only after it becomes severe.
teaching: Report new numbness, burning pain, weakness, fever, or delayed rash/shortness of breath.
delegationScope: Paclitaxel infusion requires oncology competency and emergency-response readiness.
examTrap: Assuming premedication means anaphylaxis can no longer occur.
oneLinePearl: Paclitaxel: watch the infusion now and the nerves later.

title: Trastuzumab: HER2 Therapy With Cardiac Surveillance
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Trastuzumab targets HER2 but can reduce left-ventricular function and cause infusion or pulmonary reactions. Cardiac surveillance, infusion monitoring, pregnancy prevention counseling, and rapid escalation of dyspnea or heart-failure findings are essential.
recognize: Risk of cardiomyopathy is higher with concurrent or prior anthracycline exposure.
Infusion reactions can include fever/chills but severe respiratory or hemodynamic reactions require urgent management.
priorities: Verify HER2-directed treatment plan and current cardiac-monitoring status.
Monitor infusion reaction signs and assess dyspnea, edema, weight gain, fatigue, and cough.
assessMonitor: Trend LVEF as ordered, BP, heart-failure symptoms, infusion tolerance, and pulmonary status.
interventions: Follow the oncology protocol for holding/escalating therapy when cardiac function declines or severe reactions occur.
medicationSafety: Current labeling carries boxed warnings for cardiomyopathy, infusion reactions, embryo-fetal toxicity, and pulmonary toxicity.
Cardiac risk is not eliminated by a normal baseline LVEF.
teaching: Report shortness of breath, swelling, sudden weight gain, or severe infusion-related symptoms; follow pregnancy-prevention guidance.
delegationScope: Biologic antineoplastic infusion requires facility-specific oncology competency; cardiac/pulmonary deterioration needs immediate escalation.
examTrap: Treating new edema and dyspnea as ordinary fatigue because the baseline cardiac study was normal.
oneLinePearl: HER2 therapy needs heart surveillance before symptoms become heart failure.

title: Bleomycin: Pulmonary Toxicity Outranks the CBC
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Bleomycin's signature serious toxicity is pneumonitis that can progress to pulmonary fibrosis. New cough, dyspnea, hypoxemia, or pulmonary changes require prompt evaluation even when blood counts are relatively preserved.
recognize: Pulmonary toxicity can occur at lower cumulative exposure and in younger patients, although risk rises with age and cumulative dose.
A severe early idiosyncratic reaction with hypotension, fever/chills, wheezing, or confusion can occur, especially in lymphoma treatment.
priorities: Assess baseline/current respiratory symptoms and oxygenation.
Escalate new cough, dyspnea, hypoxemia, or acute systemic reaction promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory status, ordered imaging/PFT or diffusion testing, renal/hepatic function, skin/mucosal effects, and cumulative exposure.
interventions: Coordinate perioperative history so prior bleomycin exposure is known to anesthesia/surgical teams.
medicationSafety: Avoid assuming a low cumulative dose rules out lung toxicity.
High oxygen exposure can be clinically relevant in previously treated patients, so perioperative teams need the history.
teaching: Report new cough or breathlessness immediately and tell future anesthesia teams about prior bleomycin exposure.
delegationScope: Chemotherapy administration requires specialty competency; new respiratory findings require licensed-nurse assessment and oncology escalation.
examTrap: Waiting for severe hypoxemia before reporting a new dry cough after bleomycin.
oneLinePearl: Bleomycin's red flag is the lung, not just the lab count.
sourceBasis: DailyMed bleomycin prescribing information current 2026 review

title: Etoposide: Myelosuppression and Infusion-Rate Hypotension
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Etoposide can cause severe dose-limiting myelosuppression and transient hypotension when infused too rapidly. Safe care requires CBC surveillance, infection/bleeding precautions, and controlled infusion with BP monitoring.
recognize: Neutrophil and platelet nadirs occur after treatment rather than immediately.
Lightheadedness or hypotension during infusion can be rate-related.
priorities: Review CBC and infection/bleeding findings before treatment.
Monitor BP during IV administration and slow/stop per protocol if hypotension occurs.
Escalate febrile neutropenia, major bleeding, or severe hypersensitivity.
assessMonitor: Trend CBC, BP during infusion, infection, bleeding, mucositis, nausea/vomiting, and infusion tolerance.
interventions: Administer by controlled infusion according to product/protocol requirements.
medicationSafety: Rapid IV administration increases hypotension risk.
Current 2026 labeling retains a severe-myelosuppression boxed warning for newer etoposide products.
teaching: Report fever, chills, unusual bruising/bleeding, or severe dizziness promptly.
delegationScope: Chemotherapy infusion requires specialty competency; hypotension and cytopenia complications require immediate licensed assessment.
examTrap: Pushing etoposide faster to make up lost infusion time despite falling blood pressure.
oneLinePearl: With etoposide, protect the marrow and respect the infusion rate.

title: Tamoxifen: Estrogen Blockade With Clot and Uterine Risk
bottomLine: Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen-receptor modulator used in estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer and selected risk-reduction settings. High-yield safety issues are venous thromboembolism/stroke risk, endometrial cancer/abnormal uterine bleeding, cataracts, and important drug interactions.
recognize: Unilateral leg swelling, sudden dyspnea/chest pain, focal neurologic symptoms, or unexplained uterine bleeding require evaluation.
Hot flashes and vaginal symptoms may be common but should not normalize dangerous bleeding or clot symptoms.
priorities: Review clot/stroke history, uterine status/symptoms, vision changes, and interacting medications.
Escalate thromboembolic symptoms, focal neurologic deficits, or postmenopausal/unexplained uterine bleeding.
assessMonitor: Trend adherence, thrombotic symptoms, abnormal bleeding, vision concerns, and oncology follow-up.
interventions: Reinforce mobility and individualized clot-risk reduction measures when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Tamoxifen can increase risk of endometrial cancer, venous thromboembolism, and stroke in some populations.
Review CYP2D6-interacting antidepressants with prescriber/pharmacist when relevant.
teaching: Report clot/stroke symptoms and any abnormal uterine bleeding promptly; keep oncology and gynecologic follow-up.
delegationScope: Routine administration/teaching reinforcement may be within PN scope; new bleeding or thrombotic findings require licensed assessment and provider escalation.
examTrap: Reassuring a postmenopausal patient that new vaginal bleeding is an expected tamoxifen effect.
oneLinePearl: Tamoxifen helps the breast but raises the red flags for clot and uterine bleeding.
sourceBasis: DailyMed tamoxifen citrate prescribing information and medication guide current 2026 review
